claims.text: The as-cast AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy is ductile and contains an FCC matrix and a B2 intermetallic phase.
The as-cast alloy has a random chemical distribution, low local chemical order, low APBE, and relatively smooth phase boundaries.
Aging at 600°C for 100–500 hours is sufficient to induce significant local chemical-order evolution in AlCoCrFeNi2.1.
Aging at 750°C disorders the chemically ordered state.
The brittle state contains near-stoichiometric Ni3Al-like L12 ordered domains in the FCC matrix.
The brittle state contains jagged B2/FCC phase boundaries.
Increasing local chemical order raises or maximizes antiphase-boundary energy.
Local chemical order substantially modulates stacking-fault energy.
High APBE together with low SFE favors planar slip and restricts cross-slip in the aged AlCoCrFeNi2.1 alloy.
A chemically ordered, high-APBE energy landscape forces dislocations to move by intermittent nanoscale segment detrapping rather than smooth cross-slip.
Jagged B2/FCC interfaces create localized stress concentrations at their serrations.
The combination of planar slip bands and stress concentration at jagged interfaces triggers brittle fracture.
Higher-temperature aging reduces the coherence or degree of local chemical order and lowers APBE.
Higher-temperature aging smooths B2/FCC interface serrations.
Reduced ordering and smoother interfaces at high temperature restore cross-slip and ductility.
After aging at 600°C, room-temperature elongation will fall below 5%.
The 600°C-aged state will exhibit L12 superlattice reflections in the FCC matrix.
The 600°C-aged state will have an APBE above 100 mJ/m².
After aging at 750°C, room-temperature elongation will exceed 15%.
The transition occurs when chemical ordering makes APBE exceed the critical condition for cross-slip and when interface-serration amplitude exceeds a crack-nucleation threshold.

contradictions.description: The main hypothesis places reversible disordering and interface smoothing at temperatures greater than 750°C, whereas the intervention, mechanism, and predicted outcome assign these changes to aging at exactly 750°C.

The intervention describes 600°C aging followed by 750°C aging as a sequential treatment, while the falsification experiment describes 600°C and 750°C samples as comparative aged states; it is unclear whether the 750°C specimen is independently aged or is the previously embrittled specimen.
